subject: Pilot token inventory & throughput: post-call clarifications and next steps
messages:
From: Chloe Martin <chloe.martin@redwood.com>
To: Alex Moreno <alex.moreno@parcelnexus.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 14:02:00 -0700
Subject: Pilot token inventory & throughput: post-call clarifications and next steps

Alex — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and the asks we discussed so we have a shared view before we size the pilot.

What we heard (call highlights):
- Target latency: p95 <= 300–350ms for interactive flows (you mentioned 350ms as the absolute ceiling).
- Workload mix: ~80% short interactive requests (single-turn, 40–200 tokens); ~20% multi-turn streaming sessions (1–2 minutes).
- Steady-state QPS: ~350–450 qps (you said average across US peak hours ~400 qps).
- Peak windows: short crests up to ~3k qps for 5–15 minutes during checkout spikes.
- Tokens per second: rough estimate from your team: 100–140k tokens/sec steady, up to ~850–950k tokens/sec at peak.

Attachments I pulled from our side to help diagnostics: sample telemetry we asked for + the sketch we drew on the call. Please add the traffic capture if you can.
- 20261020-pilot-telemetry-sample.csv (attachment stub)
- ParcelNexus-workload-sketch.png (attachment stub)

Action items / asks we agreed on:
1) ParcelNexus: share a 72-hour sample capture (redact PII) and a small replayable window that includes one peak crest; file formats: raw request logs or the JSON sample you mentioned.
2) Redwood (Chloe / Marissa): produce a first-draft sizing estimate for a pilot (steady + burst headroom) and a suggested canary plan.
3) ParcelNexus: confirm retention/SLA requirements for logs + whether audio/video are part of streaming sessions (we assumed text streaming only).
4) All: sync on a pilot start target next week — Chloe will tentatively request capacity Tuesday (10/27) if we have the capture by Friday (10/23).

Follow-ups I want to call out explicitly:
- Confirmation on the p95 target (300 vs 350ms) — you said product prefers 300ms but will accept up to 350ms for initial pilot.
- Clarify session lengths inside the streaming bucket (ballpark 30–120s).

Thanks — I’ll hand to Marissa for the sizing draft once we get the capture.

—
Chloe Martin
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
chloe.martin@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0126
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Pilot token inventory & throughput: post-call clarifications and next steps

Thanks Chloe — appreciate the concise recap. Couple of clarifications and I attached a tiny sample we pulled for the team (first 30 minutes from an evening peak).

Clarifications:
- p95: product would ideally like <= 300ms, but engineering is okay accepting 350ms during pilot ramp as you noted.
- Steady-state: yes, 350–450 qps; the 400 qps is the average across the US region during business hours.
- Peak behavior: peaks come in two flavors — short, ultra-high crests (2–8 minutes) when a marketing blast lands (~2.5–3k qps), and longer elevated periods (~20–40 minutes) during sustained promos (~1.2–1.6k qps).
- Streaming sessions: mostly text streaming for real-time order updates; typical sessions are 45–90s and we expect ~180 concurrent streaming sessions at steady, spiking to ~1.2k during crest windows.
- Tokens: the sample shows mean tokens/request ~120, median ~60; your tokens/sec numbers look in the right ballpark.

Attached: sample-traffic.json (small replayable slice). I redacted user IDs per your guidance.

We can get the 72-hour capture to you by end-of-day Friday. One ask from my side: can Redwood include an estimate of when autoscaling would kick for the crest shape you saw in your internal sim? That will help us decide whether to do a canary vs. full reserved pool for the pilot.

Alex
Alex Moreno
Sr. Platform Engineer, ParcelNexus
alex.moreno@parcelnexus.com

Alex — great, thanks for the sample and the extra detail. Confirming we’ll treat the 300ms p95 as the aspirational target and 350ms as the acceptable pilot ceiling.

Updated numbers I’ll use for the sizing work (please correct me if I’ve mis-stated anything):
- Steady: 400 qps (US peak business hour average) / 120 tokens/request mean. -> ~48k tokens/sec baseline (client-side). Accounting for responses & overhead we’ll assume ~110–130k tps inbound+outbound.
- Peaks: short crests to 3k qps (2–8m), longer elevated periods to 1.5k (20–40m).
- Streaming: steady concurrency ~180 sessions (45–90s each), crest concurrency up to ~1.2k.

Next steps (confirmed):
1) ParcelNexus to send 72-hour capture by EOD Friday (10/23).
2) Redwood will run a traffic replay and post a sizing recommendation (Marissa primary). Target for the sizing draft: Monday 10/26 EOD.
3) Decide pilot guardrails: canary % (10% suggested) vs. reserved pool; Chloe to propose a canary plan once sizing draft is available.

If those dates look good I’ll book a 30m checkpoint the morning of Tuesday 10/27 to review the sizing results and the canary proposal.

—
Chloe

Subject: PNX pilot sizing - first-draft numbers

Chloe / Karthik — attaching a quick first-draft sizing estimate based on the updated numbers Alex provided and our internal replay of the 30-minute sample. This is an internal draft for the team to iterate before we share with PNX.

High-level recommendation (pilot):
- Baseline steady pool to meet 400 qps (with ~30% headroom to absorb sustained variability): target capacity = equivalent of 6 quantized T4-style GPU nodes (estimate assumes model variant with 8-bit quantization and streaming-friendly kernels).
- Burst handling: autoscale policy to add capacity on crest detection; expected peak capacity to handle 3k qps crest -> ~12 GPU-equivalents needed (this includes KV cache warmup accounting and safety margin).
- Token/sec translation: steady tokens/sec ~120k (end-to-end), peak tokens/sec ~900k — these line up with the sample once response sizes are included.
- Streaming concurrency: baseline concurrency headroom for 180 steady streaming sessions; crest buffer to 1.2k via autoscale + short-term burst queuing.

Assumptions & caveats:
- Numbers assume quantized model and that prefix caching is available for repetitive system prompts (if PNX uses sessionized system prompts heavily, effective throughput improves).
- Cold-start of KV caches during a crest will temporarily reduce capacity; recommend a short warmup window in the canary plan or a small reserved buffer.
- If PNX expects hard p95 <= 300ms during crests, we should consider a small reserved pool (partial reservation) to ensure latency SLOs while autoscale ramps.

Ask: Chloe — can you confirm whether PNX prefers a canary-first approach (10% traffic, observe for two peaks) or wants to start with a small reserved buffer? I’ll convert this into a slide + an xlsx (pnx-sizing-estimate-v1.xlsx) for the engagement doc.

—
Marissa Cole
